summary: Documents the values assigned from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, such as protocol and port numbers. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1700.

plainLanguage.summary: This document is a phone book for numbers on the Internet. It lists which number means which protocol, which port a service should listen on, which addresses are used for multicast groups, and a long series of other name tables that software has to agree on.

questions: what is the assigned numbers rfc
subtitle: The 1992 master list of protocol numbers, port numbers, multicast groups and other values that Internet protocols agree on.

tldr.problem: Protocols on the Internet agree with each other only if everyone uses the same number for the same thing: which protocol sits inside an IP packet, which port a service listens on, which multicast group a protocol uses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects the assigned values for a long series of such number spaces, from IP protocol numbers and well known ports to type-of-service codes, character sets and machine names, and records who is responsible for each one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1340 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1700.

today: RFC 1340 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1700, and the live registry now lives with IANA.

sections.title: Introduction and Data Notations
sections.content:
The RFC documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. It states that it will be updated periodically, and that in any case current information can be obtained from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. Anyone developing a protocol or application that requires the use of a link, socket, port or protocol is asked to contact IANA to receive a number assignment.

Most of the protocols mentioned in the document are documented in the RFC series of notes, and some of the items listed are undocumented. In the entries below, the name and mailbox of the responsible individual is indicated. The bracketed entry, for example [nn,iii], at the right hand margin of the page indicates a reference for the listed protocol, where the number cites the document and the letters cite the person, using a NIC Ident as used in the WhoIs service.

The document also sets out its notation conventions. The convention in the documentation of Internet protocols is to express numbers in decimal and to picture data in "big-endian" order, that is, fields are described left to right with the most significant octet on the left and the least significant octet on the right. The order of transmission of the header and data described in the document is resolved to the octet level: whenever a diagram shows a group of octets, the order of transmission of those octets is the normal order in which they are read in English. Whenever an octet represents a numeric quantity, the left most bit in the diagram is the high order or most significant bit, and the bit labelled 0 is the most significant bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry says who to ask for a new number and which document explains the thing the number is for.

sections.title: Special Addresses and Protocol Numbers
sections.content:
The first registry covers IP addresses that have a special meaning. There are five classes of IP address, Class A through Class E, and Class E addresses are reserved for experimental use. A gateway which is not participating in these experiments must ignore all datagrams with a Class E destination IP address, and ICMP Destination Unreachable or ICMP Redirect messages must not result from receiving such datagrams.

Using the notation IP-address ::= { Network-number, Host-number } or { Network-number, Subnet-number, Host-number }, with "-1" meaning the field contains all 1 bits, the document lists the common special cases. The address {0, 0} means this host on this network and can only be used as a source address. {0, Host-number} is a specified host on this network, also source only. {-1, -1} is the limited broadcast, which can only be used as a destination address, and a datagram with this address must never be forwarded outside the (sub-)net of the source. {Network-number, -1} is a directed broadcast to the specified network, and {Network-number, Subnet-number, -1} a directed broadcast to the specified subnet, both destination only. {Network-number, -1, -1} is a directed broadcast to all subnets of a specified subnetted network. Finally {127, any} is the internal host loopback address, which should never appear outside a host.

The next registry is the version numbers. The Internet Protocol has a 4-bit field to identify the version of the internetwork general protocol. The assigned values are 0 Reserved, 1 to 3 Unassigned, 4 for IP, the Internet Protocol, 5 for ST, ST Datagram Mode, 6 to 14 Unassigned, and 15 Reserved.

The protocol numbers registry assigns the 8-bit Protocol field of the Internet Protocol. Among the assigned values are 1 for ICMP, Internet Control Message; 2 for IGMP, Internet Group Management; 3 for GGP, Gateway-to-Gateway; 4 for IP in IP encapsulation; 5 for ST, Stream; 6 for TCP, Transmission Control; 17 for UDP, User Datagram; 88 for IGRP; 89 for OSPFIGP; 94 for IPIP, IP-within-IP Encapsulation Protocol; and 97 for ETHERIP, Ethernet-within-IP Encapsulation. The range 99 to 254 is unassigned and 255 is reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IP addresses mean something special, such as this host or the whole broadcast range. And one byte in every IP packet says which protocol it carries, so those byte values have to be handed out too.

sections.title: Well Known and Registered Port Numbers
sections.content:
The Well Known Ports are controlled and assigned by IANA and, on most systems, can only be used by system or root processes, or by programs executed by privileged users. Ports are used in TCP to name the ends of logical connections which carry long term conversations. For the purpose of providing services to unknown callers, a service contact port is defined; the list specifies the port used by the server process as its contact port, sometimes called the well-known port. To the extent possible, the same port assignments are used with UDP.

The document notes how the range grew. The assigned ports use a small portion of the possible port numbers. For many years the assigned ports were in the range 0 to 255; more recently the range for assigned ports managed by IANA has been expanded to the range 0 to 1023.

The table assigns both a TCP and a UDP port for each service, where the same number serves both. Examples from the table: port 0 is Reserved; 1 is tcpmux, TCP Port Service Multiplexer; 7 is echo; 9 is discard; 13 is daytime; 17 is qotd, Quote of the Day; 19 is chargen, Character Generator; 20 is ftp-data, File Transfer Default Data, and 21 is ftp, File Transfer Control; 23 is telnet; 25 is smtp, Simple Mail Transfer; 37 is time; 42 is nameserver, Host Name Server; 43 is nicname, Who Is; 53 is domain, Domain Name Server; 67 is bootps, Bootstrap Protocol Server, and 68 is bootpc, Bootstrap Protocol Client; 69 is tftp, Trivial File Transfer; and 70 is gopher. A separate table follows for registered ports above that range.
sections.plainLanguage: A port number is how a client finds the service it wants on a machine. The low numbers are reserved for the standard services so that everyone can guess them.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses and Other Number Spaces
sections.content:
The document next assigns the Internet multicast addresses. Host Extensions for IP Multicasting specifies the extensions required of a host implementation of the Internet Protocol to support multicasting, and the current addresses are listed. The low group holds 224.0.0.0 Reserved, 224.0.0.1 All Systems on this Subnet, 224.0.0.2 All Routers on this Subnet, 224.0.0.4 DVMRP Routers, 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for OSPFIGP All Routers and OSPFIGP Designated Routers, and 224.0.0.9 RIP2 Routers. A second group holds 224.0.1.1 for NTP, Network Time Protocol, and 224.0.1.4 for VNP. The range 232.x.x.x is for VMTP transient groups. These addresses are listed in the Domain Name Service under MCAST.NET and 224.IN-ADDR.ARPA, and when used on an Ethernet or IEEE 802 network the 23 low-order bits of the IP multicast address are placed in the low-order 23 bits of the Ethernet or IEEE 802 net multicast address 1.0.94.0.0.0.

Other registries in the document assign recommended Type-of-Service values for the important Internet protocols. There are four assigned TOS values, low delay, high throughput, high reliability and low cost, and in each case the value indicates "better". Only one TOS value or property can be requested in any one IP datagram. The recommended values include 1000 for TELNET, for FTP control, for TFTP and for the SMTP command phase, 0100 for FTP data and for the SMTP data phase, 0000 for a DNS TCP query and for BOOTP, 0001 for NNTP to minimize monetary cost, and 0010 for any IGP and for SNMP to maximize reliability. The IP time to live parameter has a current recommended default of 64.

The remaining sections assign values in a long series of other number spaces: domain system parameters, BOOTP parameters, network management parameters, MILNET logical addresses, link numbers and X.25 address mappings, IEEE 802 numbers of interest, Ethernet numbers of interest and vendor address components, Ethernet multicast addresses, XNS protocol types, protocol and type field assignments, PRONET 80 type numbers, point-to-point protocol field assignments, address resolution protocol parameters, reverse address resolution protocol operation codes, dynamic reverse ARP, inverse address resolution protocol, X.25 type numbers, public data network numbers, telnet options, mail encryption types, MIME types, character sets, machine names, system names, protocol and service names, terminal type names, documents and people.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast groups, the priority hint in the IP header and the default time-to-live all get fixed numbers, and then a long series of name tables follow, from MIME types to the names of terminals.

sections.title: How the Numbers Are Assigned and Kept
sections.content:
The RFC is a status report rather than a procedure. It documents the currently assigned values, says that it will be updated periodically, and says that in any case current information can be obtained from the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. Anyone developing a protocol or application that requires the use of a link, socket, port or protocol is asked to contact IANA to receive a number assignment.

The responsible individual is named for each entry, along with a reference to the document that defines the protocol, so that a reader can go from a number to its specification and to the person who owns it.

The document closes with a one-line security section. Security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is a snapshot. IANA holds the live version, and anyone who needs a new number asks IANA for one.
